identity.title: LoongRL: Reinforcement Learning for Advanced Reasoning over Long Contexts

problem.claim: Enable language models to perform advanced reasoning over long contexts.

gap.claim: Advanced long-context reasoning patterns remain largely unexplored, while high-difficulty reinforcement-learning data are scarce.

contributions.claim: LoongRL, a data-driven reinforcement-learning method for advanced long-context reasoning.
KeyChain transforms short multi-hop QA into difficult long-context tasks by hiding questions within distracting documents using UUID chains.
The authors report that KeyChain-based RL induces a plan–retrieve–reason–recheck pattern that generalizes beyond training length.

stated_novelty.claim: The paper presents LoongRL as a method specifically targeting advanced long-context reasoning through synthesized high-difficulty RL data.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that models trained at 16K effectively solve 128K tasks without prohibitive full-length RL rollout costs.
On Qwen2.5-7B and 14B, the authors report absolute long-context multi-hop QA gains of 23.5% and 21.1%, respectively.
The authors report a 74.2 score for LoongRL-14B, near o3-mini at 74.5 and DeepSeek-R1 at 74.9; they also report passing all 128K needle-in-a-haystack tests while preserving short-context reasoning.

narrative_sequence.summary: Long-context reasoning is important, but its advanced reasoning patterns and suitable difficult RL data are underexplored.
LoongRL introduces KeyChain, which embeds hidden questions and UUID chains among distracting documents to create difficult long-context tasks.
RL on KeyChain data is reported to induce plan–retrieve–reason–recheck behavior that extends beyond the training context length.
The authors report substantial QA gains, near-frontier-model scores, improved retrieval, 128K stress-test success, and retained short-context reasoning.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a deliberately structured task transformation—hidden questions, distractors, and chained retrieval—to an emergent multi-stage reasoning pattern under RL.

lessons.interpretation: A training-data construction can make the intended reasoning stages necessary rather than merely describing them as objectives.
lessons.application: When proposing a reasoning method, design training examples whose solution process requires the target intermediate behaviors, then state the behavior-to-task correspondence explicitly.
lessons.exception: This may be unsuitable when the target task lacks a reliable synthetic transformation or when imposed intermediate steps distort natural problem solving.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify evaluation datasets, baseline definitions, sample sizes, statistical variation, or the exact meaning of the reported percentage gains.
Details supporting the claims about emergent reasoning, retrieval improvement, and preservation of short-context abilities are not provided.
The abstract does not establish independent verification of the reported comparisons or stress-test results.
